original.title: Development as Freedom
original.note: Record dated 2009 (later printing of the 1999 book).

core_idea: Judge well-being and development by what people are actually able to do and to be (capabilities) and what they achieve (functionings), not only by income or resources. Two people with the same income may have very different real freedoms. For Sen, expanding freedom is both the main goal and the main means of development.
key_concepts_note: Use the concepts already stored for this theory in the library (theories.concepts).
when_to_use: What can people in a given group actually do or be, and what stops them?
How should a policy or programme be evaluated beyond income or access figures?
Typical data: interviews on valued 'beings and doings', participatory methods, multidimensional survey indicators.
common_mistakes: Confusing capabilities (real freedoms) with functionings (achieved outcomes).
Listing capabilities without explaining how and why you selected them.
Treating it as the same as human capital theory.

development.adds: Proposes a list of central human capabilities, developed through the lives of women in India.
An accessible restatement of the approach for policy and research.
Methods for selecting and valuing capabilities in poverty reduction projects.
A method for measuring multidimensional poverty, later used for global poverty indices.

strands.name: Open-ended (Sen) vs list-based (Nussbaum)
strands.summary: Whether capabilities should be chosen through public reasoning or fixed in a list.

strengths.point: A broad, interdisciplinary framework for evaluating well-being, policies and social arrangements across several dimensions.

source.title: The Capability Approach: a theoretical survey

strengths.point: Separates means (resources) from ends (what people can do), which sharpens evaluation questions.

source.title: The Capability Approach: a theoretical survey

critiques.point: Too individualistic: groups shape well-being, values and choices, so group capabilities should be analysed too.
Sen's approach under-theorizes the social structures people live within.
